title: Gross specimens (museum)
ref: Robbins Basic Pathology (systemic chapters); Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology

items.name: Acute appendicitis
gross: Appendix is swollen and turgid.
Serosa is dull, granular and congested, with a coating of fibrinopurulent exudate.
Lumen may contain pus or a faecolith; mucosa may be ulcerated.
In gangrenous appendicitis the wall becomes green-black and may perforate.
keyPoints: Classic cause: luminal obstruction (faecolith, lymphoid hyperplasia) → raised pressure → ischaemia → bacterial invasion.
Histological criterion: neutrophils infiltrating the muscularis propria.
Example of acute (purulent) inflammation.

viva.q: What is the histological hallmark of acute appendicitis?
viva.a: Neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria.

viva.q: Name two complications.
viva.a: Perforation with peritonitis, and periappendiceal abscess (also pylephlebitis, rarely).

items.correction: PDF lists only swelling and congestion. Added the fibrinopurulent serosal exudate, luminal pus/faecolith and gangrenous stage, which examiners expect.

items.name: Adenocarcinoma of colon
gross: Right (caecum, ascending colon): polypoid, exophytic, fungating, soft friable mass projecting into the lumen; rarely obstructs.
Left (descending, sigmoid): annular 'napkin-ring' constricting growth with heaped-up edges and central ulceration; narrows the lumen.
Cut section: grey-white tumour infiltrating the bowel wall.
keyPoints: Right-sided tumours present with fatigue and iron-deficiency anaemia (occult bleeding); left-sided with change in bowel habit and obstruction.
Adenoma–carcinoma sequence: APC → KRAS → TP53; second pathway: mismatch-repair defects / microsatellite instability (Lynch syndrome).
CEA is used to monitor recurrence, not to screen.

viva.q: Why do left-sided colon cancers obstruct?
viva.a: They grow as annular napkin-ring lesions in a narrower colon with solid stool.

viva.q: Which tumour marker is used for follow-up?
viva.a: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA).

items.name: Atherosclerosis of aorta
gross: Intimal surface opened out.
Fatty streaks: flat or minimally raised yellow spots and streaks; do not obstruct flow.
Atheromatous plaques: raised white-to-yellow lesions (about 0.3–1.5 cm) that may coalesce.
Complicated plaques: ulceration/rupture, overlying thrombus, haemorrhage into the plaque and calcification.
keyPoints: Order of involvement: abdominal aorta > coronary arteries > popliteal arteries > internal carotids > circle of Willis.
Plaque = fibrous cap over a necrotic core (lipid, cholesterol clefts, foam cells, debris).
Chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury.

viva.q: Which part of the aorta is most affected?
viva.a: The abdominal aorta (more than the thoracic aorta).

viva.q: Name the components of an atheromatous plaque.
viva.a: Fibrous cap (smooth muscle, collagen), necrotic core (lipid, cholesterol clefts, foam cells, debris), and a shoulder with inflammatory cells and neovascularisation.

items.correction: PDF calls plaques 'white, firm'. Robbins describes atheromatous plaques as white-to-yellow; added complicated-plaque changes and the site order.

items.name: Carcinoma cervix
gross: Growth at the cervix: exophytic (fungating, cauliflower-like), ulcerative, or endophytic/infiltrative (diffusely enlarged, bulky 'barrel-shaped' cervix).
Cut section: grey-white tumour infiltrating the cervical wall, may extend to the parametrium.
keyPoints: Most are squamous cell carcinomas; adenocarcinoma is the next most common.
High-risk HPV (16, 18) — arises in the transformation zone from precursor CIN / squamous intraepithelial lesions.
Spread to the parametrium can block the ureters → hydronephrosis and renal failure.

viva.q: Which HPV types are high risk?
viva.a: 16 and 18 (most important); also 31, 33, 45 and others.

viva.q: Where does cervical cancer begin?
viva.a: In the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction).

items.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of penis
gross: Usually on the glans or inner prepuce.
Exophytic papillary, cauliflower-like growth, or a flat ulcerating/infiltrative (endophytic) lesion.
Cut section: grey-white tumour invading the shaft.
keyPoints: Risk factors: uncircumcised men, phimosis, poor hygiene/smegma, HPV 16/18, smoking.
Precursor carcinoma in situ: Bowen disease, erythroplasia of Queyrat, bowenoid papulosis.
Spreads first to inguinal lymph nodes.

viva.q: Why is penile carcinoma rare in circumcised men?
viva.a: Circumcision prevents accumulation of smegma and chronic irritation and lowers HPV persistence.

viva.q: First lymph nodes involved?
viva.a: Superficial inguinal nodes.

items.name: Chronic pyelonephritis
gross: Kidney is irregularly scarred; when bilateral, involvement is asymmetric.
Coarse, discrete, U-shaped corticomedullary scars overlying dilated, blunted or deformed calyces — scars are commonest at the upper and lower poles.
Pelvis and ureter may be dilated (reflux).
keyPoints: Two forms: reflux nephropathy (most common) and chronic obstructive pyelonephritis.
Microscopy: 'thyroidisation' of tubules — dilated tubules filled with colloid-like casts.
Contrast: chronic glomerulonephritis and benign nephrosclerosis give symmetric, finely granular kidneys.

viva.q: How do you tell chronic pyelonephritis from chronic glomerulonephritis grossly?
viva.a: Pyelonephritis: asymmetric coarse scars over deformed calyces. GN: symmetric, diffusely and finely granular contracted kidneys with normal calyces.

items.name: Chronic venous congestion of liver (nutmeg liver)
gross: Liver is enlarged, firm, with a tense capsule.
Cut surface: 'nutmeg' pattern — red-brown, slightly depressed congested centrilobular areas alternating with paler tan (sometimes fatty) periportal liver.
keyPoints: Cause: right-sided heart failure (also hepatic vein obstruction).
Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes are most hypoxic → atrophy or necrosis; periportal cells show fatty change.
Long-standing cases may develop 'cardiac sclerosis' (centrilobular fibrosis).

viva.q: Why are centrilobular hepatocytes the first to die?
viva.a: They are farthest from the oxygenated blood entering at the portal tracts (zone 3) and lie next to the congested central veins.

items.name: Fatty liver (hepatic steatosis)
gross: Liver is enlarged and heavy, with rounded margins.
Soft, greasy and yellow, with a tense, glistening capsule.
Cut surface bulges and feels greasy.
keyPoints: Commonest causes: alcohol and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome); also protein malnutrition, toxins (CCl4), pregnancy, Reye syndrome.
Reversible cell injury — intracellular accumulation of triglycerides.
Microscopy: clear vacuoles push the nucleus aside (macrovesicular); confirm fat with Oil Red O or Sudan stains on frozen sections.

viva.q: Which special stain shows fat and why can't it be used on routine paraffin sections?
viva.a: Oil Red O / Sudan III; paraffin processing uses solvents that dissolve fat, so frozen sections are needed.

items.name: Fibroadenoma of breast
gross: Well-circumscribed, round to ovoid, rubbery, freely mobile nodule (the 'breast mouse'), usually 1–4 cm.
Cut surface: grey-white, bulging, with slit-like spaces.
keyPoints: Most common benign breast tumour; young women (20s–30s).
Biphasic: proliferation of both stroma and glands (intracanalicular and pericanalicular patterns).
May enlarge in pregnancy and regress after menopause.

viva.q: What are the two growth patterns of fibroadenoma?
viva.a: Intracanalicular (stroma compresses ducts into slits) and pericanalicular (ducts stay open and round).

items.correction: PDF says 'well encapsulated'. Robbins describes it as well-circumscribed and sharply demarcated, not truly encapsulated (Harsh Mohan does use 'encapsulated'). In a viva, 'well-circumscribed' is the safer answer.

items.name: Dry gangrene of foot
gross: Affected part is dry, shrunken (mummified) and dark brown-black.
A sharp line of demarcation (line of separation) between gangrenous and viable tissue, caused by inflammation at the junction.
Spreads slowly from the distal end.
keyPoints: Cause: gradual arterial occlusion with intact venous drainage — atherosclerosis, diabetes, Buerger disease, frostbite.
Mechanism: coagulative necrosis with little bacterial putrefaction.
Black colour: iron sulphide formed from breakdown of haemoglobin.

viva.q: Differentiate dry from wet gangrene.
viva.a: Dry: arterial occlusion, limbs, shrunken black, clear line of demarcation, slow, little infection. Wet: venous + arterial obstruction, bowel/moist tissue, swollen, no clear line, putrefaction, rapid, high mortality.

items.name: Carcinoma stomach
gross: Exophytic: polypoid or fungating mass projecting into the lumen.
Ulcerative: ulcer with heaped-up, beaded, irregular margins and a shaggy necrotic base (unlike a benign peptic ulcer).
Diffuse infiltrative (linitis plastica, 'leather-bottle stomach'): rigid, thickened wall with flattened rugae.
keyPoints: Lauren classification: intestinal type (H. pylori, gland-forming) and diffuse type (signet-ring cells, loss of E-cadherin/CDH1).
Risk factors: H. pylori, nitrosamines/smoked and salted foods, chronic atrophic gastritis.
Signs of spread: Virchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Krukenberg tumour (ovaries).

viva.q: What is linitis plastica?
viva.a: Diffuse-type gastric carcinoma infiltrating the whole wall, making it rigid and thickened like a leather bottle.

viva.q: Krukenberg tumour?
viva.a: Bilateral ovarian metastases of signet-ring cell carcinoma, classically from the stomach.

items.name: Leiomyoma of uterus (intramural)
gross: Sharply circumscribed, round, firm, grey-white mass; often multiple.
Cut surface: characteristic whorled pattern; bulges and 'shells out' easily (no true capsule).
Sites: intramural, submucosal or subserosal.
keyPoints: Most common benign tumour in women; benign smooth-muscle tumour.
Oestrogen-dependent; shrinks after menopause. Common mutation: MED12.
Degenerations: hyaline (most common), cystic, red (carneous, typical in pregnancy), calcification.

viva.q: What is red degeneration?
viva.a: Haemorrhagic infarction of a fibroid, usually in pregnancy, causing pain.

viva.q: Does a leiomyoma turn into leiomyosarcoma?
viva.a: Almost never — leiomyosarcomas arise de novo.

items.name: Lipoma
gross: Soft, yellow, well-encapsulated mass with a thin capsule.
Cut surface: yellow, greasy and lobulated.
keyPoints: Most common soft-tissue tumour of adults.
Mature adipocytes with no atypia.
Usually subcutaneous on the trunk, neck and proximal limbs.

viva.q: What is the most common soft-tissue tumour in adults?
viva.a: Lipoma.

items.name: Cirrhosis of liver
gross: Liver is usually shrunken in end-stage disease (may be normal or enlarged early), firm, with a diffusely nodular surface.
Micronodular: nodules less than 3 mm (classically alcohol). Macronodular: nodules more than 3 mm (classically viral hepatitis).
Cut surface: grey-brown or yellow-tan regenerative nodules separated by grey-white fibrous septa.
keyPoints: Definition: diffuse process with fibrosis (bridging septa) and regenerative nodules that destroy normal lobular architecture.
Fibrosis comes from activated hepatic stellate cells (TGF-β).
Complications: portal hypertension (varices, ascites, splenomegaly), liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma.

viva.q: Size cut-off between micronodular and macronodular cirrhosis?
viva.a: 3 mm. Micronodular < 3 mm, macronodular > 3 mm.

viva.q: Which cell lays down collagen in liver fibrosis?
viva.a: The activated hepatic stellate (Ito) cell.

items.correction: Your notes have this reversed (they say micronodules > 3 mm and macronodules < 3 mm). Correct: micronodules are under 3 mm, macronodules over 3 mm.

items.name: Lobar pneumonia (grey hepatisation)
gross: Uniform consolidation of a whole lobe — firm, airless and liver-like.
Grey hepatisation: dry, grey-brown cut surface.
Pleura often covered by fibrinous or fibrinopurulent exudate (pleuritis).
keyPoints: Four stages: congestion → red hepatisation → grey hepatisation → resolution.
Grey colour: lysis of red cells with persisting fibrinosuppurative exudate.
Most common organism: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

viva.q: List the stages of lobar pneumonia.
viva.a: Congestion, red hepatisation, grey hepatisation, resolution.

viva.q: Name two complications.
viva.a: Lung abscess, empyema, organisation into fibrous tissue, bacteraemic spread (meningitis, endocarditis).

items.name: Mucinous cystadenoma of ovary
gross: Large cystic mass with a smooth outer surface; can be huge.
Multilocular — many cysts of varying size.
Cysts filled with sticky, thick gelatinous mucin.
keyPoints: Lined by tall columnar mucin-secreting epithelium without cilia.
Usually unilateral — far less often bilateral than serous tumours.
Pseudomyxoma peritonei usually comes from an appendiceal mucinous tumour, not the ovary.

viva.q: Serous vs mucinous cystadenoma — two differences?
viva.a: Serous: usually unilocular, clear watery fluid, ciliated tubal-type lining, more often bilateral. Mucinous: multilocular, sticky mucin, non-ciliated mucinous lining, usually unilateral and larger.

items.name: Multinodular goitre
gross: Asymmetric, multilobulated enlargement of the thyroid; can be very large.
Cut surface: many nodules of varying size containing brown gelatinous colloid.
Regressive changes: haemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification and cystic change.
keyPoints: Results from recurrent episodes of hyperplasia and involution — commonly due to iodine deficiency.
Most patients are euthyroid; a nodule may become autonomous (toxic multinodular goitre / Plummer disease).
Mass effects: airway compression, dysphagia, superior vena cava syndrome; may extend retrosternally.

viva.q: Is a multinodular goitre a neoplasm?
viva.a: No — it is a hyperplastic (adaptive) response to TSH stimulation, mostly from iodine deficiency.

items.name: Myocardial infarction with mural thrombus
gross: Infarct in the left ventricular wall; appearance depends on age: 1–3 days yellow-tan, 3–7 days with a red hyperaemic border, 7–10 days soft yellow-tan centre (rupture risk), 2–8 weeks grey-white scar forming from the edge.
Healed infarct: thin, grey-white, firm fibrous scar.
Mural thrombus: friable, laminated thrombus stuck to the endocardium over the infarct (often at the apex), with lines of Zahn.
keyPoints: Coagulative necrosis of myocardium; healed by scar (cardiac muscle is permanent tissue).
Mural thrombus forms because of endocardial injury plus stasis from a non-contracting wall.
Risk: systemic embolism (stroke, limb, kidney, spleen infarcts).

viva.q: When is the risk of cardiac rupture highest after MI?
viva.a: About 3–7 days, when the infarct is softest (macrophages removing dead muscle).

viva.q: Why does a mural thrombus form?
viva.a: Endothelial (endocardial) injury plus stasis — two parts of Virchow's triad.

items.correction: PDF describes only the healed scar, but the jar label is 'MI with mural thrombi'. Added the mural thrombus and the age-of-infarct timeline.

items.name: Osteosarcoma (osteogenic sarcoma)
gross: Bulky, gritty, grey-white tumour in the metaphysis of a long bone — commonest around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia).
Cut surface: grey-white with haemorrhage, necrosis and cystic change.
Destroys the cortex and lifts the periosteum into a soft-tissue mass.
keyPoints: Defining feature: tumour cells make osteoid (malignant bone).
Bimodal age: under 20 years; and older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation.
Genes: RB1 (hereditary retinoblastoma) and TP53 (Li-Fraumeni). Spreads by blood, mostly to the lungs.
X-ray: Codman triangle and 'sunburst' pattern.

viva.q: What is the diagnostic histological feature?
viva.a: Osteoid or bone produced directly by malignant tumour cells.

items.name: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell)
gross: Solitary, spherical, bosselated mass, most often at a pole (commonly the upper pole).
Cut surface: variegated — bright yellow (lipid-rich clear cells) to grey-white, with haemorrhage, necrosis, cystic change and calcification.
May grow into the renal vein as a solid column, sometimes up the inferior vena cava.
keyPoints: Clear cell type: loss of VHL on chromosome 3p.
Classic triad (uncommon together): haematuria, flank pain, palpable mass.
Paraneoplastic: polycythaemia (erythropoietin), hypercalcaemia (PTHrP), hypertension, Cushing syndrome.

viva.q: Why is clear-cell RCC yellow?
viva.a: Its cells are full of lipid and glycogen.

viva.q: Which gene is lost?
viva.a: VHL tumour suppressor on chromosome 3p.

items.correction: PDF omits the bright-yellow colour and renal-vein invasion, the two features examiners ask about most. Added both.

items.name: Seminoma testis
gross: Testis is enlarged by a bulky, soft, well-demarcated tumour.
Cut surface: homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated.
Usually without haemorrhage or necrosis (their presence suggests a non-seminomatous component).
keyPoints: Most common germ cell tumour of the testis; peak in the 30s.
Microscopy: sheets of large clear cells divided by fibrous septa with lymphocytes; granulomas may be present.
Very radiosensitive; AFP normal; hCG mildly raised in some (syncytiotrophoblast cells). Risk: cryptorchidism.

viva.q: Which marker would make you doubt a pure seminoma?
viva.a: Raised AFP — it points to a yolk sac (non-seminomatous) component.

items.name: Serous cystadenoma of ovary
gross: Smooth, glistening outer surface.
Usually unilocular, thin-walled cyst.
Contains clear to pale-yellow watery (serous) fluid.
keyPoints: Lining: ciliated columnar epithelium like the fallopian tube.
Bilateral more often than mucinous tumours.
Psammoma bodies are typical of serous tumours (more in malignant ones).

viva.q: Which ovarian tumour shows psammoma bodies?
viva.a: Serous tumours (especially serous carcinoma).

items.name: Squamous cell carcinoma of skin (foot)
gross: Large exophytic, cauliflower-like growth, or an ulcer with raised, everted edges.
Cut surface: grey-white tumour infiltrating deeper tissues.
keyPoints: Microscopy: nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
Risk factors: sunlight (UV), arsenic, immunosuppression, HPV, chronic scars, burns, ulcers and sinuses.
SCC arising in a chronic scar or ulcer is called a Marjolin ulcer.

viva.q: What is a Marjolin ulcer?
viva.a: Squamous cell carcinoma arising in a long-standing scar, burn, ulcer or sinus.

viva.q: Which edge is typical of a malignant ulcer?
viva.a: Raised and everted.

items.name: Tuberculous lymphadenitis
gross: Enlarged lymph nodes matted together (periadenitis).
Cut surface: grey-white with cheesy, yellow-white areas of caseous necrosis; may calcify.
May soften into a cold abscess and drain through a sinus.
keyPoints: Example of caseous necrosis and of granulomatous inflammation.
Microscopy: caseating epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells; Ziehl–Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli.
Cervical nodes are most often involved (scrofula).

viva.q: What type of necrosis is seen?
viva.a: Caseous necrosis — cheesy, structureless, granular pink material surrounded by a granuloma.

items.name: Bronchiectasis
gross: Usually bilateral, lower lobes, most severe in the distal bronchi and bronchioles.
Airways are dilated (cylindrical, fusiform or saccular) and can be followed right up to the pleural surface.
Lumens filled with mucopurulent secretions; cut surface looks cystic ('honeycomb-like').
Overlying pleura may be fibrotic and adherent.
keyPoints: Permanent dilatation of bronchi from destruction of muscle and elastic tissue by chronic necrotising infection.
Causes: obstruction (tumour, foreign body), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener), necrotising pneumonia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.
Symptoms: chronic cough with copious foul sputum.

viva.q: Which lobes are usually affected?
viva.a: The lower lobes, bilaterally (upper lobes in cystic fibrosis and ABPA).

items.correction: PDF lists only fibrotic pleura and a 'honeycomb' cut surface. The defining feature — dilated bronchi traceable to the pleura, mainly in the lower lobes — was missing. ('Honeycomb lung' on its own usually refers to end-stage interstitial fibrosis.)

items.name: Emphysema
gross: Lungs are pale and voluminous, often overlapping the heart.
Large air spaces visible on the cut surface.
Subpleural bullae (air spaces over 1 cm) and blebs.
keyPoints: Permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with wall destruction, without obvious fibrosis.
Centriacinar: smokers, upper lobes. Panacinar: α1-antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes. Paraseptal (distal acinar): subpleural, can cause spontaneous pneumothorax.
Mechanism: protease–antiprotease and oxidant–antioxidant imbalance.

viva.q: Which type of emphysema is linked to α1-antitrypsin deficiency?
viva.a: Panacinar, mainly lower lobes.

items.name: Splenomegaly (enlarged spleen)
gross: Spleen is enlarged and heavier than normal (normal adult about 150 g); massive splenomegaly exceeds 1000 g.
Congestive splenomegaly (portal hypertension): firm, capsule thickened, cut surface dark red-blue; may show Gamna–Gandy bodies (fibrosis with haemosiderin and calcium).
Infiltrative causes give a pale or uniformly fleshy cut surface.
keyPoints: Massive splenomegaly: chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelofibrosis, chronic malaria, kala-azar, Gaucher disease, hairy cell leukaemia.
Can cause hypersplenism (cytopenias) and splenic infarcts.

viva.q: Name three causes of massive splenomegaly common in India.
viva.a: Chronic malaria, kala-azar and chronic myeloid leukaemia (also thalassaemia, myelofibrosis).

items.correction: PDF says only 'increased size and weight'. Added the normal weight, cut-surface features and causes so it can be described in a spotter exam.

items.name: Infarct of spleen
gross: Pale (anaemic, white) infarcts, often multiple.
Wedge-shaped, with the base on the capsule and the apex pointing to the hilum (the occluded vessel).
Margins sharply defined with a red, congested (hyperaemic) rim early; later shrink into a depressed scar.
keyPoints: Pale infarcts occur with arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial supply (spleen, kidney, heart).
Coagulative necrosis.
Causes: emboli from the heart (mural thrombus, infective endocarditis), sickle cell disease, massive splenomegaly.

viva.q: Why are infarcts wedge-shaped?
viva.a: The occluded vessel is at the apex and the tissue it supplies fans out to the organ surface.

items.name: Madura foot (mycetoma)
gross: Swollen, deformed foot.
Multiple sinuses discharging pus with granules (grains).
Underlying bone may be destroyed.
keyPoints: Triad: painless swelling, draining sinuses, grains.
Grain colour depends on the organism: black grains — fungal (eumycetoma, e.g. Madurella mycetomatis); white/yellow or red grains — usually actinomycetoma (Nocardia, Actinomadura).
Chronic granulomatous infection entering through a thorn prick in barefoot workers.

viva.q: What do black grains suggest?
viva.a: Eumycetoma (fungal), e.g. Madurella.

items.correction: PDF says the sinuses discharge 'black granules' as if always so. Black grains mean fungal (eumycetoma); bacterial actinomycetoma gives white, yellow or red grains.

items.name: Giant cell tumour of bone (osteoclastoma)
gross: Eccentric tumour in the epiphysis of a long bone (often extending into the metaphysis), commonest around the knee.
Large, red-brown, soft, with haemorrhage and cystic change.
Expands the bone, which is surrounded by a thin shell of reactive bone.
keyPoints: Age 20–40 years, after the growth plates close.
Microscopy: osteoclast-like giant cells scattered among mononuclear stromal cells that express RANKL (treated with denosumab).
Locally aggressive; often recurs after curettage; X-ray shows a lytic 'soap-bubble' lesion.

viva.q: Which part of the bone is involved?
viva.a: Epiphysis, extending to the metaphysis.

items.name: Papillary carcinoma of thyroid
gross: Solitary or multifocal; firm, grey-white.
May be well-circumscribed or even encapsulated, or show infiltrative margins.
Cut surface may show papillary foci, cystic change, fibrosis and calcification.
keyPoints: Most common thyroid cancer (about 85%).
Diagnosis rests on nuclei: Orphan Annie eye (optically clear) nuclei, nuclear grooves, intranuclear pseudo-inclusions; psammoma bodies.
Genes: BRAF V600E, RET/PTC rearrangements; risk factor: radiation. Spreads to cervical lymph nodes; excellent prognosis.

viva.q: Which nuclear features clinch the diagnosis?
viva.a: Ground-glass (Orphan Annie eye) nuclei, nuclear grooves and pseudo-inclusions.

items.name: Chronic peptic ulcer
gross: Small (usually under 2–3 cm), round to oval, sharply punched-out ulcer.
Margins level with the surrounding mucosa (not heaped up); clean, smooth base.
Mucosal folds radiate towards the ulcer like spokes of a wheel.
keyPoints: Sites: first part of duodenum (most common), lesser curvature of stomach near the antrum–body junction.
Causes: H. pylori, NSAIDs; also Zollinger–Ellison syndrome.
Complications: bleeding (most common), perforation, pyloric obstruction.

viva.q: How do you tell a benign from a malignant gastric ulcer grossly?
viva.a: Benign: punched-out, flat margins, clean base, folds radiating to the edge. Malignant: heaped-up/beaded margins, shaggy necrotic base, folds interrupted.

items.name: Renal stones with hydronephrosis
gross: Dilated renal pelvis and calyces.
Progressive thinning of the cortex and medulla (pressure atrophy) — eventually a thin-walled cystic sac.
Dilated ureter when the block is lower down; stones in the pelvis or ureter.
keyPoints: Most stones are calcium oxalate; struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) forms staghorn stones with urease-producing organisms like Proteus; also uric acid and cystine.
Hydronephrosis = dilatation of the pelvis and calyces with parenchymal atrophy from obstruction to urine outflow.
Parenchymal loss is an example of pressure atrophy.

viva.q: Which stone forms a staghorn calculus?
viva.a: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), with urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus.

items.correction: PDF lists only dilated pelvis/calyces and ureter. Added cortical atrophy, the feature that makes it hydronephrosis rather than simple dilatation.

items.name: Mature cystic teratoma of ovary (dermoid cyst)
gross: Usually unilocular cyst lined by skin-like wall.
Contents: hair, greasy sebaceous material, teeth, cartilage, bone.
A raised nodule in the cyst wall — Rokitansky protuberance (head/nipple) — where most tissues arise.
keyPoints: Most common ovarian germ cell tumour; young women.
Tissues from all three germ layers, all mature.
Complications: torsion, rupture, rarely malignant change (usually squamous cell carcinoma); struma ovarii contains thyroid tissue.

viva.q: What is the Rokitansky protuberance?
viva.a: A solid nodule projecting into a dermoid cyst from which hair, teeth and other tissues arise.

items.name: Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)
gross: Large, solitary, well-circumscribed mass in the kidney.
Cut surface: soft, homogeneous, tan to grey, with foci of haemorrhage, cystic change and necrosis.
keyPoints: Most common primary renal tumour of childhood (2–5 years); presents as an abdominal mass.
Triphasic microscopy: blastemal, stromal and epithelial elements.
Genetics: WT1 (11p13) — WAGR and Denys–Drash syndromes; WT2 region (11p15) — Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome.

viva.q: Name the three components of Wilms tumour.
viva.a: Blastema, stroma and epithelium (tubules, abortive glomeruli).

items.correction: PDF has a photo but no description. Added gross features and key points.

items.name: Osteochondroma
gross: Mushroom-shaped bony outgrowth with a stalk.
Capped by glistening blue-white hyaline cartilage.
Arises from the metaphysis near the growth plate (often around the knee); the stalk's cortex and marrow are continuous with the parent bone.
keyPoints: Most common benign bone tumour.
Solitary, or multiple in hereditary multiple exostoses (EXT1/EXT2 mutations).
Rarely transforms into chondrosarcoma — more often in the hereditary form.

viva.q: What is unique about the marrow cavity of an osteochondroma?
viva.a: It is continuous with the marrow cavity of the underlying bone.

items.correction: PDF has a photo but no description. Added gross features and key points.

items.name: Intestinal tuberculosis
gross: Commonest site: ileocaecal region.
Ulcerative form: transverse (girdle) ulcers running around the bowel, because they follow lymphatics; healing causes strictures.
Hyperplastic form: thickened wall forming a mass that narrows the lumen.
keyPoints: Microscopy: caseating granulomas in the bowel wall and regional nodes.
Contrast: typhoid ulcers are longitudinal, over Peyer patches, and do not cause strictures.
Differential diagnosis: Crohn disease (non-caseating granulomas, skip lesions).

viva.q: Typhoid vs tuberculous intestinal ulcers?
viva.a: Typhoid: longitudinal, along Peyer patches, no stricture. TB: transverse/girdle, following lymphatics, heal with stricture.

items.correction: PDF has a photo but no description. Added gross features and key points.

items.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
gross: Secondary (reactivation) TB: caseous lesions at the lung apex that may break into a bronchus and form cavities.
Cavities have ragged walls with caseous lining; surrounding fibrosis and pleural thickening.
Primary TB: Ghon focus (subpleural, lower part of upper lobe or upper part of lower lobe) plus caseous hilar nodes = Ghon complex.
keyPoints: Apical localisation is linked to high oxygen tension in the apices.
Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells; acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
Complications: haemoptysis, spread to other lobes (bronchopneumonia), miliary TB, empyema, amyloidosis.

viva.q: What is the Ghon complex?
viva.a: Ghon focus (subpleural parenchymal lesion) plus caseous hilar lymph nodes in primary TB; when it calcifies it is the Ranke complex.

items.name: Hydatidiform mole
gross: Mass of thin-walled, translucent, grape-like cystic structures (swollen chorionic villi).
Complete mole: no embryo or fetal parts. Partial mole: some normal villi and fetal parts may be present.
keyPoints: Complete mole: usually 46,XX, all paternal (androgenetic); very high hCG; about 2% progress to choriocarcinoma.
Partial mole: triploid (e.g. 69,XXY); lower risk.
Ultrasound shows a 'snowstorm' appearance; follow with serial β-hCG.

viva.q: What is the karyotype of a complete mole?
viva.a: Usually 46,XX, with all chromosomes from the father.

items.name: Medullary carcinoma of breast
gross: Well-circumscribed, soft, fleshy, grey-tan tumour (brain-like — hence 'medullary').
May show foci of haemorrhage and necrosis.
keyPoints: Microscopy: sheets of large pleomorphic cells with pushing borders and a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.
Often triple-negative and linked to BRCA1; prognosis better than its high grade suggests.
The current WHO classification groups it under invasive carcinoma of no special type with a medullary pattern ('carcinoma with medullary features').

viva.q: Which hereditary mutation is linked to medullary carcinoma?
viva.a: BRCA1.

items.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
gross: Enlarged prostate (often 60–100 g) with nodules in the transition (periurethral) zone.
Cut surface: many well-circumscribed nodules, grey-white to yellow-pink, which may ooze milky fluid.
Urethra compressed into a slit; a median lobe may project into the bladder.
keyPoints: Hyperplasia of glands and stroma driven by dihydrotestosterone (5α-reductase) — an adaptation, not a precursor of cancer.
Prostatic carcinoma usually arises in the peripheral zone instead.
Bladder outflow obstruction → bladder wall hypertrophy (trabeculation), diverticula, hydronephrosis.

viva.q: Which zone does BPH arise in, and which zone carcinoma?
viva.a: BPH: transition (periurethral) zone. Carcinoma: peripheral zone.

items.name: Actinomycosis
gross: Multiple interconnecting abscesses and sinus tracts in a firm, fibrotic tissue ('honeycomb' appearance when an organ such as the liver is involved).
Pus contains small yellow 'sulphur granules'.
keyPoints: Actinomyces israelii — a Gram-positive, filamentous, anaerobic bacterium (not a fungus).
Commonest form: cervicofacial ('lumpy jaw') after dental infection; also thoracic and abdominal (ileocaecal).
Granules show radiating filaments with club-shaped ends (Splendore–Hoeppli).

viva.q: Is Actinomyces a fungus?
viva.a: No — it is a Gram-positive filamentous anaerobic bacterium, though it grows like a fungus.
